Title: June 11, 2026 City Council Study Session: 2026 State Legislative Update
Overview: Intergovernmental Affairs Officer Heather Staer reviewed the outcomes of the 2026 Colorado legislative session, including state budget cuts, bills the city supported or opposed, and the November 2026 ballot measures. Council asked questions on budget and grant impacts, wildfire and utility reliability, and data center bills, and gave feedback on future advocacy timing. Council reached consensus to direct staff to return with more information on the ballot measures, including Initiative 175, before taking formal positions by resolution at a future meeting.

Topic1.Title: Session Overview and Governor Action
Topic1.Summary: The 2026 legislature met for a 120-day session from January 14 to May 13 and introduced about 626 bills, with roughly 450 sent to the governor. The governor had already vetoed 12 bills and had until the following day to act on the rest. The city took positions on 58 bills and posted a new bill tracker on its website.

Topic2.Title: State Budget Shortfall and Medicaid
Topic2.Summary: The Joint Budget Committee had to cut about one billion dollars, leaving little room for new programs, and K-12 was prioritized. Medicaid costs are outpacing state revenue and drive much of the deficit. The legislature created a commission to recommend Medicaid policy changes by December, and a budget forecast is expected in June or July.

Topic3.Title: Federal Response, Immigration Bills, and Initiative 175 Counter-Measure
Topic3.Summary: The majority party focused on responding to federal immigration policies, passing House Bill 1276 on civil liability for sharing immigration status information and detention center inspections. Election-year primaries highlighted tensions between moderate and progressive Democrats. House Bill 1430 was passed as a counter to Initiative 175, a road-funding initiative that could reduce local revenues, and proponents appear to be moving forward with the initiative.

Topic4.Title: City Priority Bills: Homelessness, AI, and Utility On-Bill Repayment
Topic4.Summary: House Bill 1202 passed, allowing multi-jurisdictional homelessness authorities and requiring a state homelessness strategy. Senate Bill 189, which clarifies city responsibilities for automated decision-making and AI, passed and was signed. Senate Bill 148, the utility on-bill repayment program, failed in appropriations after a funding error and disputes over the unclaimed property trust fund, and staff will revisit it over the interim.

Topic5.Title: Direct and Indirect Budget Impacts on the City
Topic5.Summary: The largest direct impact is the elimination of the local share of the retail marijuana sales tax, which will cost the general fund about 150,000 dollars. An amendment to preserve that share failed, though council can raise local marijuana taxes to close the gap. Multimodal transportation funding was cut by 10.5 million dollars, and affordable housing finance funding was reduced by about 130 million dollars statewide.

Topic6.Title: Dueling Data Center Bills
Topic6.Summary: House Bill 1030 would have offered data center incentives without strong energy or environmental requirements, and the city opposed it. Senate Bill 102 would have set strict requirements for large-load data centers, and the city supported it. Both bills died in committee, and the Senate Bill 102 sponsors plan to bring a new version next session.

Topic7.Title: Housing and Land Use Legislation
Topic7.Summary: The city supported Senate Bill 40, which expands the affordable homeownership program, and House Bill 1065, which creates transit and housing investment zones and a state tax credit for affordable housing. House Bill 1224 on mobile home park sales and resident fees also passed. The city opposed House Bill 1114 on minimum lot sizes and House Bill 1308 on lot splitting, and both failed in the Senate Local Government Committee.

Topic8.Title: Clean Energy Bills
Topic8.Summary: The city supported several clean energy bills, including plug-in solar, which passed. House Bill 1226, addressing federal actions on coal plants, was also supported. The city helped defeat Senate Bill 208, which would have removed wind energy from Colorado's clean energy standards.

Topic9.Title: Firearm Safety Bills
Topic9.Summary: The city opposed three bills that would have eroded local and state firearm safety laws, and all three were defeated. The city supported House Bill 1144, which adds guardrails around 3D printing of firearms, and it passed.

Topic10.Title: RTD Modernization (House Bill 1150)
Topic10.Summary: House Bill 1150 reduces the RTD board from 15 to nine members, with five elected and four appointed by the governor, and redraws district boundaries. The city sought seven elected seats, equity language in nominations, and a lower signature threshold, and only the signature threshold was restored to 250. The governor's office pointed to existing equity policies, so no additional equity language was added.

Topic11.Title: Looking Ahead: 2026 Election and 2027 Session Outlook
Topic11.Summary: Democrats are expected to keep control of the legislature after the November 2026 general election, but a new governor and new House leadership may shift priorities. The state budget remains a problem, and a special session may be needed. Staff noted that August 3 is the deadline for initiative signatures and September 2 is when the final ballot will be known.

Topic12.Title: November Ballot Measures: Initiatives 85, 95, 108, 109, and 110
Topic12.Summary: Staff described Initiative 85, which raises felony penalties for fentanyl and synthetic opioid offenses, mandates treatment for some drug felonies, and narrows exemptions. Initiative 95 requires law enforcement to notify federal immigration authorities in certain cases. Initiatives 108, 109, and 110 address child sex trafficking penalties, school athletics based on biological sex, and surgeries for minors.

Topic13.Title: Referred Measure SB 135 and Initiatives in Circulation
Topic13.Summary: Senate Bill 135 refers a measure to voters to let the state keep revenue above the TABOR cap, up to 4.8 billion dollars, for K-12 and child programs. Initiative 175 would dedicate transportation taxes and fees to roads and bridges and could reduce general fund revenue by about 540 million dollars in future years. Initiatives 177 and 195, which would add a natural gas right and a graduated income tax, are still gathering signatures.

Topic14.Title: Council Questions on Budget Impacts and Grants
Topic14.Summary: Council asked for an aggregate estimate of the city's exposure if the TABOR cap increase fails, and staff said a projection depends on state revenue forecasts and would come later in the budget process. Staff agreed to analyze Initiative 85 with the police chief, sheriff, and judge. Council also asked how Boulder's marijuana tax loss compares with other cities, and staff said the grant loss may affect Boulder more because it is a successful grant applicant.

Topic15.Title: Council Questions on Data Centers and Grants
Topic15.Summary: Council asked how close the dueling data center bills came to passing and whether local home rule policies would be preempted. Staff said Senate Bill 102 preserved local control, and both bills stalled in committee because of labor and environmental opposition. Will Coin said data center incentives are losing bipartisan support.

Topic16.Title: Wildfire Risk and Utility Reliability
Topic16.Summary: Council asked whether other communities share common goals on wildfire protection and power reliability that could support collective action. Staff said a utility civil immunity proposal was shut down last summer, and the Public Utilities Commission was reauthorized for seven years with quality-of-service plan requirements. A possible initiative, 308, could fund wildfire and forest work through a sporting goods sales tax.

Topic17.Title: Right to Natural Gas Initiative
Topic17.Summary: A council member asked why the right to natural gas initiative was pursued, and staff said similar bills have failed for years in the legislature. Staff said the measure would preempt the city's building and energy conservation codes and remove local control over natural gas limits.

Topic18.Title: Advocacy Timing and Legislative Priorities
Topic18.Summary: Council discussed when to start advocating for next year's legislation, and staff said outreach typically picks up in August and September. A council member proposed that council members send staff their ideas for legislation in July to build momentum before the fall priority-setting process. Staff noted that the election year may distract legislators.

Topic19.Title: Council Discussion of November Ballot Measures
Topic19.Summary: Council members expressed concern about several measures, particularly Initiatives 108, 109, 110, and 95, which some said could harm transgender people or people seeking reproductive care. Others said Initiative 85 needs more analysis of its effects on sentencing and treatment. Council also noted that the group behind the measures is a dark money organization that spent heavily to gather signatures.

Topic20.Title: Next Steps for Ballot Position Decisions
Topic20.Summary: Council agreed to ask staff for more information on all six ballot measures, including Initiative 175, before taking formal positions. Staff will return with research on who supports each measure and what each would affect, and it will consider positions by resolution at a future regular meeting. Council did not take a straw poll and moved on after reaching this direction.
